newsitem.title: USA: US school alters French Web pages in legal case.
newsitem.headline: US school alters French Web pages in legal case.

text.p: Georgia Institute of Technology has added multilingual translations to the Web site for its French campus even though a court in Paris on Monday rejected a lawsuit that claimed the site's exclusive use of English had violated French law.

The tribunal rejected on technical grounds a complaint that had been filed by two groups for the preservation of the French language. It did not rule on the precedent-setting question of whether France has the right to control the Internet using laws for the protection of French culture.

"The suit had a number of procedural and legal flaws," Georgia Tech president Wayne Clough said in a statement. "We are pleased that the Police Tribunal of Paris agreed with Georgia Tech Lorraine's legal position."

Teddy Puttgen, director of Georgia Tech Lorraine, said the Web site was revamped several weeks ago to include German and French translations. He said the decision had nothing to do with the pending court ruling.

A suit was filed in October by the Association for the Defence of the French Language and Future of the French Language claiming the Web site for the university's Metz campus violated the 1994 Toubon law barring the sale in France of "goods and services" in a language other than French.
The university initially defended its Web site, saying it was not feasible to translate pages into French if they were exclusively intended for an English-speaking audience.

"We have argued that the Internet is very different from overall advertisement in that when you actually visit a site you enter that virtual domicile. And once you have entered that virtual domicile we are then free to actually communicate in any particular language and fashion we so desire," Puttgen said.
He said he expected the two French groups to appeal the court's decision. Supporters of the French language have complained that about 90 percent of all Internet communication is in English.
